messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

message.content:
At 10 kPa the equilibrium freezing point of pure water is essentially unchanged from its normal value at atmospheric pressure.  
**Freezing point ≈ 0 °C (≈ 273 K)** – the pressure dependence is only on the order of 10⁻⁴ °C per kPa, so even at 10 kPa the shift is less than 0.001 °C.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?" They want the freezing point of water at 10 kPa. The freezing point of water depends on pressure. At standard atmospheric pressure (~101.3 kPa), freezing point is 0°C. At lower pressures, freezing point decreases slightly. At 10 kPa, it's about -2°C? Actually, the freezing point depression with pressure is small. The Clapeyron equation: dT/dP = TΔV / ΔH. For water, ΔV (solid-liquid) is negative? Actually, water expands when freezing, so ΔV = V_solid - V_liquid > 0? Wait, water has larger volume as ice, so ΔV = V_solid - V_liquid > 0. So dT/dP = TΔV/ΔH. ΔH is latent heat of fusion ~ 6.01 kJ/mol. T ~ 273 K. ΔV ~ 1.9 cm^3/mol? Actually, molar volume of ice ~ 19.6 cm^3/mol, liquid ~ 18.0 cm^3/mol, so ΔV ~ 1.6 cm^3/mol. Convert to m^3/mol: 1.6e-6 m^3/mol. So dT/dP = 273 * 1.6e-6 / 6010 J/mol? Wait, ΔH ~ 6.01 kJ/mol = 6010 J/mol. So dT/dP = 273 * 1.6e-6 / 6010 = (436.8e-6)/6010 = 7.27e-8? Actually, 436.8e-6 = 0.0004368. Divided by 6010 gives 7.27e-8 K/Pa. Multiply by 1000 Pa to get 7.27e-5 K/kPa. So per kPa, temperature changes by ~7.3e-5 K. So at 10 kPa difference from 101.3 kPa, difference ~ 10 * 7.3e-5 = 0.00073 K. So negligible. So freezing point at 10 kPa is essentially 0°C. But maybe at 10 kPa, water is supercooled? Actually, at 10 kPa, water can remain liquid below 0°C until it reaches the homogeneous nucleation temperature (~-40°C). But the equilibrium freezing point is still ~0°C. So answer: ~0°C. But we can mention that the freezing point is essentially unchanged at 10 kPa, around 0°C. So answer: ~0°C.
